result.overall: The Court granted Mr. Senadheerage's application for judicial review, finding the RAD's decision unreasonable due to unsupported implausibility findings and improper requirements for corroboration, and remitted the matter for redetermination.

themes.name: Implausibility Findings
themes.summary: The Court found the RAD's implausibility findings were speculative and lacked a firm evidentiary basis, making them unreasonable.

themes.name: Requirement for Corroboration
themes.summary: The Court clarified the legal framework for requiring corroboration, emphasizing that it cannot be a general requirement and must be justified with independent reasons and procedural safeguards.

themes.name: Assessment of Corroborative Evidence
themes.summary: The Court found the RAD reasonably rejected some corroborative evidence but failed to address other relevant evidence, contributing to the unreasonableness of the decision.

themes.name: Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) Analysis
themes.summary: The Court held the RAD improperly conflated the IFA analysis with the persecution analysis, failing to assume a well-founded fear of persecution for the IFA assessment.

themes.name: Standard of Review and Reasonableness
themes.summary: The Court applied the Vavilov reasonableness standard, requiring a rational chain of analysis and compliance with legal constraints.

arguments.quote: Mr. Senadheerage challenges the RAD’s assessment of his evidence.
arguments.claim: The RAD erred in finding his story implausible, in rejecting his corroborative evidence and in requiring additional corroboration.

arguments.quote: The RAD found that there was insufficient evidence that either the CID or the businessman’s thugs had any remaining interest in harming Mr. Senadheerage.
arguments.claim: There was insufficient evidence that the CID or the businessman’s thugs had any remaining interest in harming Mr. Senadheerage.
arguments.outcome_note: Court found the implausibility findings speculative and unsupported.

arguments.quote: The RAD also confirmed the RPD’s analysis with respect to the IFA.
arguments.claim: Confirmed the RPD’s finding that Mr. Senadheerage had an internal flight alternative in two cities where his family relocated.
arguments.outcome_note: Court found the IFA analysis improperly conflated with persecution analysis.

arguments.quote: The Minister, however, argues that the RAD’s IFA finding stands independently of its conclusion regarding Mr. Senadheerage’s lack of a well-founded fear of persecution.
arguments.claim: The IFA finding is an independent and sufficient ground to uphold the RAD’s decision, regardless of errors in the persecution analysis.
arguments.outcome_note: Court found the IFA analysis was not independent and could not sustain the decision.

holdings.quote: I am granting his application, for two inter-related reasons.
holdings.statement: The application for judicial review is granted due to unreasonable implausibility findings and improper requirements for corroboration.

holdings.quote: the decision itself must be justified, not only justifiable.
holdings.statement: A decision must exhibit a rational chain of analysis and comply with legal constraints (Vavilov framework).

holdings.quote: This Court, however, has set a high threshold before immigration decision-makers can make a finding of implausibility.
holdings.statement: Implausibility findings may only be made in the clearest of cases, where facts are outside the realm of reasonable expectation or contradicted by documentary evidence.

holdings.quote: the RAD did not explain the basis for its implausibility findings.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s implausibility findings were speculative and lacked evidentiary support, making them unreasonable.

holdings.quote: Thus, I find that this aspect of the RAD’s decision is unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s implausibility findings are unreasonable.

holdings.quote: the RAD appears to have started from the premise that there is a general requirement for corroboration.
holdings.statement: The RAD erred by treating corroboration as a general requirement without proper justification.

holdings.quote: A decision-maker can only require corroborative evidence if: The decision-maker clearly sets out an independent reason for requiring corroboration...
holdings.statement: Corroboration may only be required if there is an independent reason and the evidence could reasonably be expected to be available, with an opportunity for explanation.

holdings.quote: I find that some aspects of the RAD’s analysis with respect to corroboration are unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s approach to corroboration was unreasonable.

holdings.quote: it was unreasonable for the RAD to require corroboration with respect to the death threats.
holdings.statement: The RAD failed to provide sufficient explanation for requiring corroboration of the death threats.

holdings.quote: the RAD appears to have reversed the two-step approach outlined above and focused on the presumptive availability of corroborative evidence as a ground for requiring corroboration.
holdings.statement: The RAD improperly reversed the corroboration analysis and failed to provide procedural fairness.

holdings.quote: the RAD may have required corroboration because of its flawed implausibility findings, instead of a desire to buttress the trustworthiness of hearsay.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s corroboration requirement was tainted by its flawed implausibility findings.

holdings.quote: the RAD’s conclusions were not unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD reasonably gave little weight to certain corroborative evidence (newspaper article and lawyer’s letter).

holdings.quote: The RAD should have responded to this argument. Its failure to do so may not, alone, have rendered its decision unreasonable. Nonetheless, it contributes to the decision’s overall unreasonableness.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s failure to address a relevant letter contributed to the overall unreasonableness.

holdings.quote: the RAD’s analysis of the evidence is flawed in many respects.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s analysis of the evidence is fundamentally flawed and unreasonable.

holdings.quote: the RAD confused the two issues, at least in significant part.
holdings.statement: The RAD improperly conflated the IFA and persecution analyses.

holdings.quote: I cannot sustain the decision on the basis of the IFA finding.
holdings.statement: The IFA finding cannot independently sustain the RAD’s decision.

holdings.quote: the application for judicial review will be allowed and the matter will be sent back for redetermination.
holdings.statement: The application is allowed and the matter is remitted for redetermination.

rebuttals.point: The IFA finding is an independent and sufficient ground to uphold the RAD’s decision, regardless of errors in the persecution analysis.
rebuttals.court_answer: The IFA analysis was not independent and was tainted by the same errors as the persecution analysis.

authorities.quote: the standard of review is reasonableness: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov].
authorities.authority: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
authorities.why: Sets the standard of review and requirement for a rational chain of analysis.

authorities.quote: Such a finding may be made only in the “clearest of cases:” Valtchev v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 776 [Valtchev];
authorities.authority: Valtchev v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 776
authorities.why: Establishes the high threshold for implausibility findings.

authorities.quote: He noted that “the unusual or improbable does occur, and that it is unreasonable to reject evidence as not credible simply because the events it describes are unusual:” Al Dya, at paragraph 35.
authorities.authority: Al Dya v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 901
authorities.why: Clarifies that unusual events are not inherently implausible.

authorities.quote: the well-known presumption of truthfulness established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Maldonado v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 FC 302 at 305 (CA)
authorities.authority: Maldonado v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 FC 302 (CA)
authorities.why: Presumption of truthfulness unless there is reason to doubt.

authorities.quote: Corroborative evidence was only required if the RAD had (1) reason to doubt the Applicants’ claim and (2) the corroborating evidence could reasonably be expected to be available […].
authorities.authority: Horvath v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 CF 147
authorities.why: Sets out the two-step approach for requiring corroboration.

authorities.quote: when corroborative evidence should reasonably be available to establish the essential elements of a refugee protection claim and there is no reasonable explanation for its absence, the administrative decision maker may draw a negative inference
authorities.authority: Fatoye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 456
authorities.why: Describes the exception for requiring corroboration when evidence should reasonably be available.
